listeningParts.title: Registering with a medical practice
listeningParts.contextDescription: A student phones a doctors' surgery to register as a new patient.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Good morning, Parkview Medical Centre, Anita speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Hi, I've just moved here to start a postgraduate course at the university, and I'd like to register with your practice.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Of course. First, I need to check that you live within our area. What's your address?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: It's Flat 7, 22 Belmont Road.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Belmont Road, yes, that's within our boundary. Have you been registered with a doctor in this country before?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: No, this is my first time. I'm from the United States.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: That's fine. You'll need to fill in a registration form, which you can do online or on paper here at the surgery. We'll also need to see some proof of your address, such as a tenancy agreement or a letter from the university, and your passport.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: I have a letter from the university confirming my accommodation. Would that be okay?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Perfect. Once you've registered, we'll invite you for a short health check with one of our nurses. It's not compulsory, but we recommend it. The nurse will check your blood pressure, ask about any medical conditions and make sure your vaccinations are up to date.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That sounds useful. Actually, that reminds me, I take medication for asthma. How do I get my prescriptions here?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: When you register, please bring the details of your medication, ideally the packaging or a letter from your doctor at home. You'll need to see one of our doctors first, and then you can order repeat prescriptions online through our app, and collect them from any pharmacy.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Is there a charge for prescriptions?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: In England, there's a standard charge for each item, but if you need a lot of medication regularly, you can buy a prepayment certificate, which works out cheaper. The pharmacist can explain the details.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Okay. And how do I make an appointment to see a doctor?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: There are three ways. You can phone us from eight in the morning, use the online booking system, or come to the desk in person. For urgent problems, we keep some same-day appointments, but they go quickly, so it's best to call as soon as we open. For routine appointments, you might have to wait a week or so.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: And what if I need medical help in the evening or at the weekend?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The surgery is closed then, but you can call the national helpline, one-one-one, any time of the day or night. They'll tell you where to go, and they can arrange for you to see a doctor if necessary. For a serious emergency, like chest pain or severe bleeding, you should call nine-nine-nine or go straight to the hospital.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That's really helpful. Is there anything for students specifically?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, the university health service runs a mental health and well-being clinic on Wednesday afternoons, here in our building. It's free for students, and you can book directly without seeing a doctor first. A lot of students find it helpful, particularly in the first term.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Good to know. What are your opening hours?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Monday to Friday, eight until six thirty. And on Tuesday evenings, we stay open until eight for people who work during the day.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Is it easy to get to the surgery by public transport? I don't have a car.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, the number twelve bus stops right outside, and it's about a fifteen-minute walk from the main university campus. There's also a small car park and space for bicycles at the back of the building, if you decide to get a bike later.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: And can I choose which doctor I see?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: You'll be registered with the practice as a whole, but you can ask to see a particular doctor when you book. We have six doctors, three men and three women, and two of them speak other languages as well as English, if that's ever helpful.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Great. Can I start the registration now?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: I can take some basic details. What's your full name?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Megan Kowalski. K-O-W-A-L-S-K-I.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: And your date of birth?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: The fourteenth of March, two thousand and one.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you. I'll send you a text with the link to the online form. Once we've received it and checked your documents, it usually takes about three working days to complete the registration.

listeningParts.title: A museum of medical history
listeningParts.contextDescription: A guide introduces visitors to a museum of the history of medicine.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, and welcome to the Halloran Museum of Medicine. My name is Ciara, and I'll be introducing you to the museum before you explore on your own. The museum is housed in what was once the city's first public hospital, built in 1745, so you're standing in a building that has its own place in medical history.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The collection was started by a surgeon, Dr Thomas Halloran, who worked here in the nineteenth century. He collected instruments, specimens and documents, partly for teaching his students and partly because he believed that future generations should understand how medicine had developed. When he died, he left his collection to the hospital, and it was opened to the public as a museum in 1935, after the hospital moved to a new site.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Let me explain how the museum is organised. There are five galleries, arranged in chronological order. Gallery One, on the ground floor to your left, covers ancient and medieval medicine, including some remarkable surgical instruments from Roman times that look surprisingly similar to modern ones.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Gallery Two is devoted to anatomy. For centuries, doctors' understanding of the body was based on the writings of the ancient Greek physician Galen, many of which turned out to be wrong, because Galen had mainly dissected animals rather than humans. This gallery shows how, from the sixteenth century, anatomists began to study human bodies directly. Some visitors find a few of the exhibits here rather disturbing, so there's a separate route that avoids this gallery if you prefer.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Upstairs, Gallery Three is the old operating theatre, which is the highlight for many visitors. Before the discovery of anaesthetics in the 1840s, operations were performed while patients were fully conscious, so surgeons had to work as fast as possible. A good surgeon could remove a leg in under a minute. Students watched from the steep wooden seats around the room, which you can still see today. Every Saturday at two o'clock, we have a demonstration here, with an actor playing a Victorian surgeon. It's very popular, so please collect a free ticket from the front desk.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Gallery Four tells the story of the fight against infectious disease, from the first vaccine against smallpox, developed by Edward Jenner in 1796, to the discovery of penicillin in 1928. There's an interactive display where you can look at bacteria through a microscope, which children especially enjoy.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: And finally, Gallery Five looks at modern medicine and the future, including robotic surgery and genetic medicine. It also includes a section on the recent pandemic, with objects and personal stories donated by local healthcare workers.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Now, a few practical points. Photography is allowed in all galleries, but please don't use flash, as it can damage older items. Bags larger than a small backpack must be left in the cloakroom, which is free. There's a café in the courtyard, and the gift shop is next to the exit.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: If you're visiting with children, we have a free activity trail, which you can pick up at the front desk. Children follow clues around the galleries and collect stamps, and when they finish they receive a small badge. The trail takes about forty-five minutes and is designed for ages six to twelve. We also run family workshops during school holidays, where children can try making their own herbal remedies, using the same plants that apothecaries sold two hundred years ago.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The museum is fully accessible. There's a lift to the first floor next to the cloakroom, and wheelchairs can be borrowed free of charge. Seating is available in every gallery if you need a rest, and the courtyard is a pleasant place to sit on a sunny day.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: If you'd like to know more about any object, scan the code next to it with your phone for a short audio description. Audio guides are also available to borrow from the front desk for three euros, with versions in six languages. Enjoy your visit.

listeningParts.title: Evaluating a public health campaign
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two public health students, Grace and Sam, discuss their evaluation of a campaign to encourage hand-washing in schools.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: So, Sam, we need to finish the analysis for our report on the hand-washing campaign. Have you looked at the absence figures?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yes. Just to remind ourselves, the campaign ran in ten primary schools for one term, and we compared them with ten similar schools that didn't take part. The main outcome we measured was how many days pupils were absent because of illness.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: And the result?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: In the campaign schools, sickness absence fell by about eighteen per cent compared with the same term the previous year. In the comparison schools, it fell by about six per cent.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: So the comparison schools also improved. Why do you think that was?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Probably because the previous winter had a particularly bad flu season, so absence was unusually high that year. That's exactly why we needed the comparison group. If we'd only looked at the campaign schools, we'd have overestimated the effect.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: Right. So the real effect is the difference, roughly twelve percentage points. That's still substantial. What about the observations?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: That was more complicated. We observed pupils after break and before lunch to see if they washed their hands properly. At the start of the campaign, about forty per cent did. By the middle of the term, it had risen to over seventy per cent.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: But it dropped again towards the end, didn't it?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yes, to about fifty-five per cent. It seems the novelty wore off. The posters and songs were exciting at first, but after a few weeks, the children stopped noticing them.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: That's an important finding. It suggests campaigns need to be refreshed regularly, rather than just run once.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Agreed. The teachers' interviews were interesting too. Most of them were positive, but a few mentioned practical problems.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: Like what?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: The biggest one was soap. In several schools, soap dispensers often ran out, and nobody was clearly responsible for refilling them. One teacher said it was pointless telling children to wash their hands when there was no soap.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: So the campaign was only as good as the facilities. We should definitely recommend that schools assign someone to check supplies.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: And another teacher said there weren't enough sinks. With thirty children all trying to wash their hands before lunch, it took ages, and lunch was delayed.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: Did any teachers mention how the children themselves reacted?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yes, several said the younger children were the most enthusiastic. The five- and six-year-olds loved the hand-washing song and reminded each other to use it. The older pupils, especially the ten- and eleven-year-olds, found it a bit childish, and one teacher said they started making fun of the posters.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: That's useful. Perhaps the materials need to be adapted for different age groups. Older children might respond better to something more scientific, like growing bacteria from unwashed hands in a dish and comparing it with washed hands.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Actually, one school did exactly that in a science lesson, and the teacher said it had a much bigger impact on the older pupils than the posters did. They were quite shocked by what grew.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: I'm not surprised. Let's mention that as an example of good practice in the discussion.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: Okay. What about the limitations of our study?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Well, the schools weren't randomly chosen. The campaign schools volunteered, so their head teachers may have been especially keen on health, which could affect the results.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: Also, one term is quite short. We don't know whether the effect would last over a whole year.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: And when pupils knew they were being observed, they may have washed their hands more carefully than usual.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: Good point. That's sometimes called the observer effect. Right, I think our recommendations should be: refresh the campaign regularly, make sure facilities are adequate, and carry out a longer study with randomly selected schools.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Sounds good. I'll write the results section, and you do the discussion?

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: Deal. Let's aim to have drafts ready by Monday.

listeningParts.title: The story of antibiotics
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a microbiology course on the discovery of antibiotics and the problem of resistance.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. Today we're going to look at antibiotics: how they were discovered, how they work, and why their effectiveness is now under serious threat.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: It's hard to imagine today how dangerous bacterial infections were before antibiotics. A small cut or a scratch from a rose thorn could lead to a fatal infection. Pneumonia, tuberculosis and infections after childbirth killed millions of people. Surgery was extremely risky, not because of the operation itself, but because of the infections that often followed.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The story of the first antibiotic usually begins in 1928, in the London laboratory of the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming. Fleming was studying bacteria called staphylococci, and before going on holiday, he left several dishes of them on his laboratory bench. When he returned, he noticed that one dish had been contaminated by a mould, and that the bacteria around the mould had been killed. He identified the mould as Penicillium, and named the substance it produced penicillin.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: However, Fleming found penicillin very difficult to purify and produce in useful amounts, and he eventually turned to other research. For about ten years, little progress was made. Then, at the end of the 1930s, a team at Oxford University led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain took up the work. They developed methods of extracting and purifying penicillin, and in 1941, they treated their first patient, a policeman suffering from a severe infection. He began to recover, but the supply of penicillin ran out, and he died. The scientists had been so short of the drug that they had even recovered it from the patient's urine to use again.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The Second World War created an urgent need for penicillin to treat wounded soldiers, and production was scaled up enormously, mainly in the United States. A key breakthrough came when researchers found a strain of Penicillium growing on a mouldy melon in a market in Illinois, which produced far more penicillin than Fleming's original mould. By the end of the war, penicillin was being produced in large quantities, and Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in 1945.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Over the following decades, many other antibiotics were discovered, most of them from microorganisms found in soil. Antibiotics work in different ways: some destroy the walls that surround bacterial cells, while others prevent bacteria from making proteins or copying their DNA. Importantly, antibiotics have no effect on viruses, which is why they're useless against colds and flu.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Fleming himself warned of the main danger in his Nobel Prize speech. Bacteria reproduce extremely quickly, and occasionally random changes in their DNA, known as mutations, make some of them resistant to a particular antibiotic. When the antibiotic is used, the bacteria that aren't resistant are killed, but the resistant ones survive and multiply. Every time antibiotics are used, therefore, there's a risk of encouraging resistance. Bacteria can also pass resistance genes directly to one another, even between different species.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The problem has been made much worse by overuse. Antibiotics are often prescribed for viral infections, where they do nothing, and in many countries they can be bought without a prescription. Large quantities are also given to farm animals, not only to treat disease but to make them grow faster, although this has been banned in the European Union since 2006. Meanwhile, very few new types of antibiotic have been developed since the 1980s, partly because they're not very profitable for drug companies: a new antibiotic is used for short courses and is often kept in reserve for emergencies.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: A major study published in 2022 estimated that over a million deaths a year worldwide are directly caused by antibiotic-resistant infections. Solutions include using antibiotics more carefully, improving hygiene and vaccination to prevent infections in the first place, and finding new ways to encourage research. Next week, we'll look at some promising alternatives, including viruses that attack bacteria.

readingPassages.title: The conquest of smallpox
paragraphs: For most of recorded history, smallpox was one of the most feared diseases on Earth. It spread easily from person to person through the air, caused high fever and a painful rash that turned into fluid-filled blisters, and killed around three in every ten people it infected. Those who survived were often left with deep scars on their faces, and some were blinded. In the eighteenth century alone, it is estimated that smallpox killed around four hundred thousand Europeans every year, and in the twentieth century, before it was finally defeated, it caused an estimated three hundred million deaths worldwide.

Long before scientists understood how diseases spread, people noticed that those who recovered from smallpox never caught it again. This observation led to a practice known as variolation, in which material from the blisters of a person with a mild case was deliberately introduced into a healthy person, usually through a small cut in the skin or, in China, by blowing dried scabs into the nose. The person usually developed a mild form of the disease and was then protected for life. Variolation was practised in parts of Asia and Africa for centuries before it reached Europe.

The practice was introduced to Britain in the 1720s, largely through the efforts of Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, the wife of the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire. She had survived smallpox herself, and had seen variolation performed in Constantinople. On her return to London, she had her daughter variolated in front of the king's doctors. The method became fashionable among wealthy families, but it carried real risks. Around one or two per cent of those variolated died, and because they had a genuine infection, they could pass the disease to others.

The decisive breakthrough came from an English country doctor, Edward Jenner. It was common knowledge among farmers that milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a mild disease of cattle that caused sores on the hands, seemed to be protected against smallpox. In 1796, Jenner tested this idea. He took material from a cowpox sore on the hand of a milkmaid named Sarah Nelmes and introduced it into the arm of an eight-year-old boy, James Phipps. Some weeks later, he variolated the boy with smallpox material, and the boy did not become ill. Jenner called his method vaccination, from the Latin word vacca, meaning cow.

Jenner's experiment would not be considered ethical today, and he was not the first person to try the method; a farmer named Benjamin Jesty had used cowpox to protect his family more than twenty years earlier. Jenner's contribution was to test the idea systematically, to publish his results and to promote vaccination energetically. Vaccination was far safer than variolation, and it spread with remarkable speed. Within a few years, it was being used across Europe and the Americas. In 1803, the Spanish government sent an expedition to its colonies carrying the vaccine in a living chain of orphan boys, who were vaccinated one after another during the voyage to keep the material fresh.

Not everyone welcomed the new method. Some people objected on religious grounds, arguing that it was wrong to introduce material from animals into the human body. Cartoons of the time showed vaccinated people growing horns or the heads of cows. When the British government made vaccination of infants compulsory in 1853, opposition grew stronger, and anti-vaccination leagues were formed. By the end of the century, the law had been changed to allow parents who objected on grounds of conscience to refuse.

Despite vaccination, smallpox remained common in many parts of the world well into the twentieth century. In 1967, the World Health Organization launched an intensified campaign to eliminate the disease completely. At that time, there were still between ten and fifteen million cases a year, mainly in South America, Africa and South Asia. The campaign was helped by two features of the disease: it only infected humans, so there was no animal reservoir in which it could hide, and its rash made infected people easy to identify.

Rather than trying to vaccinate whole populations, which proved impossible in many areas, the campaign adopted a strategy called surveillance and containment. Teams searched for new cases, isolated the patients and vaccinated everyone around them, creating a ring of immunity that stopped the virus from spreading further. The last natural case occurred in Somalia in 1977, and in 1980 the World Health Organization officially declared that smallpox had been eradicated. It remains the only human disease ever to have been completely wiped out, although samples of the virus are still kept in two high-security laboratories, one in the United States and one in Russia.

readingPassages.title: The long war against malaria
paragraphs: Malaria has probably killed more people than any other disease in human history. Even today, despite more than a century of scientific effort, it infects around two hundred and fifty million people every year and kills more than six hundred thousand, most of them children under the age of five in sub-Saharan Africa. The story of the fight against malaria is a story of remarkable discoveries, disappointing setbacks and, more recently, cautious hope.

For centuries, people believed that the disease was caused by bad air rising from swamps and marshes, which is where its name comes from: the Italian words mala aria mean 'bad air'. The idea was not entirely foolish, since malaria was indeed most common near stagnant water. The real cause was discovered in 1880 by a French army doctor, Alphonse Laveran, who saw tiny parasites in the blood of a patient in Algeria. Seventeen years later, a British doctor working in India, Ronald Ross, proved that the parasites were carried by mosquitoes, a discovery that earned him the Nobel Prize in 1902.

We now know that malaria is caused by single-celled parasites of the genus Plasmodium, and that it is spread only by female Anopheles mosquitoes, which need a meal of blood to produce their eggs. When an infected mosquito bites, parasites enter the bloodstream and travel to the liver, where they multiply. They then invade red blood cells, which burst every two or three days, releasing more parasites. This cycle causes the attacks of fever, shaking and sweating that are typical of the disease. When another mosquito bites the infected person, it picks up parasites and the cycle begins again.

The first effective treatment came from South America. In the seventeenth century, Jesuit missionaries in Peru learned from local people that the bark of the cinchona tree could reduce fever. The active ingredient, quinine, was isolated by French chemists in 1820 and became the standard treatment for more than a century. It was so important that European colonial powers established cinchona plantations in Asia, and it has been said that without quinine, much of the European colonisation of Africa would not have been possible.

In the middle of the twentieth century, it seemed that malaria could be defeated altogether. Powerful new insecticides, particularly DDT, were sprayed inside homes to kill mosquitoes, and a cheap synthetic drug called chloroquine was widely used for treatment. In 1955, the World Health Organization launched a global eradication campaign. Malaria was eliminated from Europe, the United States and several other countries, and cases fell dramatically in parts of Asia. However, the campaign largely excluded sub-Saharan Africa, where the disease was most common.

By the late 1960s, the campaign was in trouble. Mosquitoes had become resistant to DDT, the parasites had become resistant to chloroquine, and concerns about the environmental effects of DDT, raised by books such as Rachel Carson's Silent Spring, led to its use being restricted. Funding dried up, and in 1969 the goal of global eradication was abandoned. In many countries, the disease returned, and by the 1990s malaria deaths in Africa were rising again.

A new effort began around the year 2000, supported by international organisations and large private donors. One of the simplest tools proved to be among the most effective: bed nets treated with insecticide, which protect people while they sleep, when Anopheles mosquitoes are most active. Hundreds of millions of nets have been distributed, and studies suggest they have prevented more cases than any other measure. At the same time, a new family of drugs based on artemisinin, a substance discovered by the Chinese scientist Tu Youyou in an ancient herbal remedy, replaced chloroquine as the main treatment. Between 2000 and 2015, malaria deaths worldwide fell by around sixty per cent.

The most recent development is the arrival of vaccines. Developing a malaria vaccine has proved extremely difficult, partly because the parasite changes its form at different stages of its life cycle. In 2021, the World Health Organization recommended the first vaccine for children, and a second, cheaper vaccine was approved in 2023. Neither is completely effective, and both require several doses, but used together with nets and drugs, they could save tens of thousands of lives each year. Yet challenges remain. Resistance to artemisinin has appeared in parts of Africa, and climate change may allow mosquitoes to spread to higher and cooler areas where malaria was previously rare.

readingPassages.title: Testing the treatments
paragraphs: How do we know whether a medical treatment works? For most of history, the answer depended on the opinion of experienced physicians, who based their judgements on the patients they had personally treated. The problem with this approach is that people often recover from illnesses naturally, so a doctor who gives a treatment and sees the patient improve may wrongly conclude that the treatment caused the recovery. As a result, many treatments that did more harm than good, such as bloodletting, remained popular for centuries.

One of the earliest recorded attempts to compare treatments fairly was made in 1747 by James Lind, a Scottish naval surgeon. Sailors on long voyages frequently suffered from scurvy, a disease that caused bleeding gums, weakness and eventually death. Lind took twelve sailors with scurvy and divided them into six pairs, giving each pair a different remedy, including vinegar, seawater and two oranges and a lemon each day. The sailors who ate citrus fruit recovered rapidly, while the others did not. Although Lind's trial was very small, it is often described as the first controlled clinical trial. Surprisingly, it was more than forty years before the British navy began to provide lemon juice to all its sailors.

The modern randomised controlled trial emerged in the mid-twentieth century. Its key feature is that patients are allocated to groups by chance, so that the groups are as similar as possible in every respect except the treatment they receive. A landmark study published in 1948 by the British Medical Research Council tested the antibiotic streptomycin for tuberculosis. Partly because the drug was in short supply, the researchers could justify giving it to only some patients, and they used random numbers to decide who would receive it. The trial demonstrated a clear benefit and is widely regarded as a model of good research design.

Randomisation alone is not enough to guarantee reliable results. If patients know they are receiving a new treatment, their expectations may influence how they feel, and if doctors know, they may unconsciously assess those patients more favourably. To avoid this, many trials are double-blind, meaning that neither patients nor researchers know who is in which group until the trial is over. The comparison group typically receives either a placebo or the best existing treatment.

In the 1970s, a British doctor named Archie Cochrane argued that doctors should base their decisions on the systematic evaluation of all the available evidence, rather than on habit or authority. He criticised the medical profession for failing to organise the results of trials in a way that would allow doctors to use them. His ideas inspired the movement known as evidence-based medicine and led to the founding in 1993 of the Cochrane Collaboration, now an international network of researchers who produce systematic reviews summarising the findings of all the reliable trials on a particular question.

Systematic reviews are important because individual trials can give misleading results. A small trial may find a positive effect simply by chance, and there is a well-documented tendency for studies with positive results to be published more often than those with negative or disappointing ones. This problem, known as publication bias, can make treatments appear more effective than they really are. One partial solution has been to require researchers to register their trials publicly before they begin, so that results which are never published can at least be identified. Since 2005, many leading medical journals have refused to publish trials that were not registered in advance.

The influence of funding is another concern. Most trials of new drugs are paid for by the companies that make them, and several studies have found that industry-funded trials are more likely to reach conclusions favourable to the sponsor's product. This does not necessarily mean that the research is dishonest; companies may, for example, choose to compare their drug with a weak alternative or to test it on patients who are most likely to benefit. Nevertheless, critics such as the British doctor and writer Ben Goldacre have argued that greater transparency, including access to full trial data, is essential if doctors and patients are to trust the evidence.

Randomised trials also have limitations of their own. They are expensive and slow, and they often exclude elderly people, pregnant women and patients with several illnesses, which means that their results may not apply to the patients doctors see in everyday practice. For this reason, researchers increasingly supplement trials with large observational studies using health records from millions of patients. Such studies can reveal rare side effects or long-term outcomes that trials are too small or too short to detect, although they cannot prove cause and effect as convincingly. In my view, the best evidence comes from combining both approaches rather than relying on either alone.
